item.text: {"facts":[{"source_id":"SRC-eda3a201f3bf463e","start_unit":6,"end_unit":7,"fact_summary":"Under Sisi, agricultural projects were dominated by the president, military-owned companies, and major national and foreign investors; small farmers and agricultural workers remained marginalized and largely absent from decisions affecting agriculture. Gulf investors received privileged access to resources and large land plots.","question_ids":["5B.4","5B.5","5B.8","6B.3","8B.6"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"Ongoing during Sisi's presidency and materially applicable in 2023; the source describes the policy pattern as continuing under the Sisi regime.","ruler_attribution":"The authors explicitly attribute the agricultural-project structure and privileged resource access to the Sisi regime and associated military and investor networks.","limitations":["The source is a secondary analytical assessment and does not provide a 2023 administrative dataset or a specific presidential directive for each project."]},{"source_id":"SRC-eda3a201f3bf463e","start_unit":9,"end_unit":9,"fact_summary":"Egyptian export-oriented irrigation projects, including New Valley/Toshka and Sharq al-Owaynat, were assessed as depleting water resources and jeopardizing long-term viability, particularly amid reductions in Nile water and non-renewable groundwater.","question_ids":["6B.6","8B.7","8B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"The projects and environmental effects predate 2023 but remained relevant to Egypt's 2023 resource and sustainability position.","ruler_attribution":"The source links the projects to Egyptian state policy; it does not attribute every project decision exclusively to Sisi.","limitations":["The passage does not quantify Sisi's personal role in initiating or modifying each project."]},{"source_id":"SRC-eda3a201f3bf463e","start_unit":11,"end_unit":12,"fact_summary":"Egypt's energy import bill rose from $8.5 billion in 2021 to $13.5 billion in 2022 and was estimated at $14 billion in 2023; the energy-subsidy budget reached 1 percent of GDP in 2023. Fiscal constraints limited public-sector hiring and unemployment remained high.","question_ids":["5B.3","5B.6","5B.9","5B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"Directly covers the 2023 estimate and 2023 subsidy budget; the preceding figures provide the trend into 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The source attributes the subsidy and fiscal-policy outcomes to the Egyptian government under Sisi, while noting the external shock from the Ukraine war.","limitations":["The source does not isolate the share of the 2023 result caused by government policy versus global energy prices."]},{"source_id":"SRC-eda3a201f3bf463e","start_unit":11,"end_unit":12,"fact_summary":"Sisi's administration reduced subsidies for energy-intensive industries and later shifted from universal to targeted energy subsidies, with 30–50 percent increases for bottled gas and electricity during the IMF-linked 2016 reform period; by 2023 social pensions were only 0.3 percent of GDP, below lower-middle-income and regional averages.","question_ids":["5B.9","6B.2","6B.3","6B.6"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The policy changes began before 2023, while the cited 2023 social-pension level directly describes the period endpoint.","ruler_attribution":"The source explicitly attributes the subsidy reforms and social-protection implementation to the Sisi administration and Egyptian authorities.","limitations":["The passage reports aggregate social-pension spending rather than beneficiary-level access or outcomes."]},{"source_id":"SRC-eda3a201f3bf463e","start_unit":13,"end_unit":13,"fact_summary":"Egypt's share of renewables in electricity production increased from 9.36 percent in 2011 to only 12 percent in 2022, leaving Egypt behind Jordan and Morocco in energy diversification and exposed to fossil-fuel price shocks.","question_ids":["5B.6","5B.9","5B.10","8B.7"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The latest quantitative observation is 2022 and informs the inherited position entering 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The source evaluates national energy policy across the period but does not assign the entire trend specifically to Sisi.","limitations":["No 2023 renewable-share figure is supplied."]},{"source_id":"SRC-eda3a201f3bf463e","start_unit":14,"end_unit":15,"fact_summary":"Egypt's public debt was reported at more than 88 percent of GDP, and the Sisi administration's development model relied on military-led megaprojects and weapons spending; cited projects included the $8 billion New Suez Canal and the $59 billion New Administrative Capital.","question_ids":["5B.1","5B.3","5B.6","5B.10","8B.2","8B.3","8B.7"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"Directly relevant to Egypt's economic position in 2023; the projects and debt accumulation span earlier years.","ruler_attribution":"The source explicitly describes the debt crisis as rooted in the state-capitalist model spearheaded by the Sisi administration and identifies military-owned firms as project leaders.","limitations":["The source presents an analytical causal interpretation; it does not provide a full counterfactual assessment of project benefits."]},{"source_id":"SRC-eda3a201f3bf463e","start_unit":15,"end_unit":15,"fact_summary":"Egypt imported $12.72 billion in arms between 2013 and 2022, imports rose by more than 200 percent in 2013–2017 compared with 2008–2012, and Egypt ranked as the world's third-largest arms importer in 2020.","question_ids":["2B.8","5B.1","8B.3"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"The figures cover the pre-2023 period and describe the military-spending trajectory inherited into 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The source connects the arms spending to the military-centered economic and political strategy under Sisi.","limitations":["The figures end in 2022 and do not establish the security necessity or effectiveness of each procurement decision."]},{"source_id":"SRC-eda3a201f3bf463e","start_unit":18,"end_unit":18,"fact_summary":"Egypt faced obligations of approximately $28 billion in maturing debt and interest and a current-account deficit by the end of 2023, plus another $20 billion in 2024, creating pressure to generate foreign-currency inflows.","question_ids":["5B.3","5B.9","5B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"Directly concerns Egypt's 2023 financing needs and the immediate 2024 pipeline.","ruler_attribution":"The source describes these as obligations confronting the Egyptian authorities under Sisi.","limitations":["The passage does not specify which obligations were incurred by Sisi's government versus inherited debt."]},{"source_id":"SRC-eda3a201f3bf463e","start_unit":18,"end_unit":18,"fact_summary":"In June 2022 Egypt announced a State Ownership Policy to reduce state participation in some sectors and increase it in others; in February 2023 the government announced plans to sell shares in 32 state-owned enterprises by March 2024, including two military-run companies.","question_ids":["5B.4","5B.5","5B.6","8B.1","8B.2","8B.6"],"polarity":"favorable","period_fit":"The policy was announced before 2023, while the 32-enterprise sale plan was announced in February 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The source attributes both the State Ownership Policy and the 2023 sale announcement to the Egyptian government under Sisi.","limitations":["The record concerns announced policy and planned implementation, not completed privatization or verified outcomes."]},{"source_id":"SRC-eda3a201f3bf463e","start_unit":18,"end_unit":19,"fact_summary":"The government repeatedly postponed opening military companies to private investors, citing technical, transparency, profitability, and legal complexities; the source concludes that authorities failed to open the companies and lacked political will to curtail military economic expansion. In early 2023 Sisi allocated new lands to the army.","question_ids":["5B.4","5B.5","5B.7","8B.6","8B.8"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"Directly covers the implementation status and land allocation during early 2023, while describing an ongoing policy pattern.","ruler_attribution":"The source explicitly attributes the new land allocation to Sisi and the broader postponement and non-implementation to the Egyptian authorities under his leadership.","limitations":["The source relies partly on expert and media assessments and does not provide the underlying land-transfer instrument or complete company-level records."]},{"source_id":"SRC-eda3a201f3bf463e","start_unit":19,"end_unit":19,"fact_summary":"The military's political veto power was described as having disrupted major UAE investments and resisted opening military companies to private investors; the source characterizes the resulting status quo as a refusal by Sisi and the military to reevaluate the military's economic role.","question_ids":["5B.5","7B.9","8B.3","8B.5","8B.8"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"The assessment concerns the Sisi-era political economy and remained relevant during 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The authors explicitly attribute the strategic stance to both Sisi and the Egyptian military, while identifying military veto power as a constraint on reform.","limitations":["This is an analytical judgment about political will and veto power, not a finding from a formal audit or court."]},{"source_id":"SRC-eda3a201f3bf463e","start_unit":20,"end_unit":21,"fact_summary":"Egypt's financial dependence on Gulf funders led it to align with leading Gulf states' political interests; the source states that funders pressured Cairo to reduce military economic involvement and improve state-enterprise transparency, producing tensions over asset valuations and delayed transfer of Tiran and Sanafir.","question_ids":["2B.1","2B.10","5B.3","5B.7","8B.9"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The account describes the continuing geopolitical and financial relationship entering and during 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The source attributes Egypt's alignment and policy responses to the Egyptian regime under Sisi, while also emphasizing the leverage exerted by external funders.","limitations":["Some cited events predate 2023, and the source does not establish that Sisi personally made every foreign-policy decision."]},{"source_id":"SRC-eda3a201f3bf463e","start_unit":22,"end_unit":22,"fact_summary":"The authors conclude that Egypt lacked a credible long-term development and economic-transformation vision, while military influence was stifling the private sector and undermining prospects for development and the shrinking middle class.","question_ids":["5B.1","5B.4","5B.10","8B.1","8B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"The conclusion evaluates Egypt's trajectory through the period ending in 2023 and its prospects thereafter.","ruler_attribution":"The source links the lack of transformation and militarization of the economy to the Egyptian governing model under Sisi.","limitations":["This is a broad expert conclusion rather than a single dated policy event or quantitative outcome."]}],"documents_with_no_material_fact":[],"batch_limitations":["The supplied source is a secondary political-economy analysis published in January 2024; several facts describe policies or trends predating 2023 but materially shape Egypt's position during 2023.","The document contains little or no direct evidence about nuclear risk, domestic detention and torture, protest policing, electoral administration, judicial independence, personal financial integrity, or formal truthfulness by Sisi; those lenses are therefore largely uncovered rather than inferred."]}
